Wisconsin Land Contracts: Seller Rules FAQ

What is a land contract?

A contract where the buyer pays over time while the seller keeps title until a set point.

How does a land contract sale work in Wisconsin?

A Wisconsin land contract lets a buyer pay the seller over time, and a deed follows once the contract is fulfilled. The seller is the vendor and the buyer is the purchaser or vendee, and the statutes and court decisions use those labels.

The contract has to be in writing. Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(e) says a contract to convey is not valid unless it is signed by or on behalf of all parties. A handshake deal or an unsigned payment ledger will not carry a property transfer.

Even though the vendor holds the deed, the vendee has real rights. The Wisconsin Supreme Court held in Steiner v. Wisconsin American Mutual Insurance Company, 2005 WI 72, that equitable title stays with the vendee until a circuit court enters an order confirming default after the redemption period ends. The official annotations to s. 846.30 summarize that holding.

What happens if the buyer stops paying on a land contract?

The vendor has to go to court, and the court must give the buyer at least 7 working days to redeem. Wis. Stat. 846.30 covers strict foreclosure of a land contract. If the court finds the buyer owes payments and failed to make them, and the vendor is entitled to strict foreclosure, it sets a redemption period of at least 7 working days from the judgment hearing or, with no hearing, from entry of the judgment order.

No strict foreclosure judgment is final until the court enters an order after the redemption period confirming that no redemption occurred. Only then does the judgment become absolute.

The annotations add that the minimum period exists to keep a court from giving the buyer no chance to redeem. A court of appeals decision listed there also holds that the right can be waived when every person who holds it agrees to waive.

Because the buyer's rights end only through that court order, a vendor who wants out of a stalled contract should ask the clerk of circuit court in the county where the property sits how a strict foreclosure case starts and what filing fee applies.

What transfer fee applies to a Wisconsin land contract?

The grantor owes the state real estate transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction, which is $3 per $1,000. Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) adds that for a land contract the value is the total principal amount the buyer agrees to pay the seller.

As an illustration only, a land contract with total principal of $120,000 produces a fee of $360 at that rate. The register of deeds collects the fee when the instrument is submitted for recording, and the grantor and grantee both sign the transfer return.

SituationFee treatmentSource
Land contract recordedFee based on total principal the buyer agrees to payWis. Stat. 77.22(1)
Deed given when the contract is paidExempt if the proper fee was paid when the contract or evidence of it was recordedWis. Stat. 77.25(17)
Foreclosure or deed in lieu to a land contract sellerExemptWis. Stat. 77.25(14)
Transfer by will, descent or survivorshipExemptWis. Stat. 77.25(11)
Fee collectionRegister of deeds collects it at recording, with a return signed by grantor and granteeWis. Stat. 77.22(1)

The definition in s. 77.21(1) counts contracts and assignments of a vendee's interest as conveyances. If a buyer sells their position to someone else, ask the register of deeds how the fee applies to that assignment.

Which disclosures must a land contract seller give?

A seller of one-to-four unit residential property by land contract must give the buyer a condition report. Wis. Stat. 709.01(1) applies the disclosure rules to transfers by sale, exchange or land contract, unless the transfer is exempt from the transfer fee.

  • The report is due no later than 10 days after acceptance of the contract of sale or option contract.
  • A buyer who gets no report in that time may rescind in writing within 2 business days after the 10-day period ends and recover deposits.
  • A report counts as complete only when the owner answered or supplied information for every item.
  • Personal representatives, trustees, conservators and court-supervised fiduciaries who never occupied the property are excused from the report.

Condominium sellers must add the association name, assessment amounts and a contact person to the report.

What if a land contract vendor or vendee dies?

The vendor's interest can pass through the register of deeds, without a court case, when the right person applies. Under Wis. Stat. 867.046(2), the decedent's spouse, a beneficiary of a marital property agreement, a transfer on death beneficiary, or a beneficiary of certain survivorship transfers can apply to the register of deeds in the county where the property sits.

  • The application for real property includes a copy of the latest property tax bill and a legal description.
  • When recorded, the application serves as prima facie evidence of the facts it recites and ends the decedent's interest.
  • If no one starts a confirmation proceeding within 90 days after death, any interested person may apply.
  • A purchaser or lender who acts in good faith and pays value takes title free of estate claims and has no duty to inquire.

Ask the register of deeds in your county for the application form and whether the office accepts it in person or by mail.

Can a land contract buyer get Wisconsin property tax credits?

A land contract buyer can qualify for the lottery and gaming credit when the home is a primary residence. The Department of Revenue says the buyer qualifies if the land contract, or an instrument evidencing it, is notarized no later than six months after the January 1 certification date.

The same page says the credit stays with a property that is sold after January 1 and should be counted when taxes are prorated between buyer and seller. The county treasurer where the property sits can tell you whether the credit appears on the current bill.

The annotations to s. 815.20 also state that a land contract vendee has an interest sufficient to support the homestead exemption, which protects up to $75,000 against creditors.

What should a land contract seller do before selling the home?

Pull the paperwork first, then decide whether to wait for the contract to finish or sell the vendor's position. A cash buyer will want to see the signed contract, the payment history and any recorded memorandum.

  • Ask the register of deeds whether the contract or a notice of it is recorded, and whether the transfer fee return was filed.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the tax bill and any credit shown on it.
  • Read the contract for any clause that limits assignment or sale before you promise anything to a new buyer.
  • Ask the county treasurer whether any taxes are past due on the parcel.

A Wisconsin real estate attorney can tell you whether strict foreclosure or a negotiated payoff fits your facts.

More questions about Wisconsin Land Contracts and Contracts for Deed

How long does a buyer have to redeem after a land contract judgment in Wisconsin?

The court must set a redemption period of at least 7 working days. Wis. Stat. 846.30 counts it from the judgment hearing or, with no hearing, from entry of the judgment order. The judgment is not final until a later order confirms that no redemption happened.

Who pays the transfer fee on a land contract?

The grantor pays it. The rate is 30 cents per $100 of value, and for a land contract the value is the total principal the buyer agrees to pay the seller. The register of deeds collects it at recording.

Is a land contract sale exempt from the condition report?

No, unless the transfer is exempt from the transfer fee or the seller is an excused fiduciary who never lived there. Wis. Stat. 709.01(1) names land contracts among the covered transfers for one-to-four unit property.

Does the buyer own the house during a land contract?

The buyer holds equitable title. A 2005 Wisconsin Supreme Court decision says equitable title stays with the buyer until a court order confirms default after the redemption period ends.

Can heirs of a land contract vendor sell the property?

They can once their interest is confirmed. The register of deeds route under Wis. Stat. 867.046 lets qualifying beneficiaries record an application, and a good-faith purchaser from them takes free of estate claims.

What the official sources say

  • The seller (grantor) pays the 30 cents per $100 real estate transfer fee, collected at recording. (Wis. Stat. 77.22(1); source)
Selling in Wisconsin?
We buy Wisconsin houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What closing costs does a Wisconsin seller pay by law?

The charges that Wisconsin statutes assign to a seller are the real estate transfer fee, the cost of recording any document the seller must record, and the duty to deliver a real estate condition report. Most other costs, such as a listing agent's commission, title charges and the proration of the year's property tax, come from the contract and the settlement statement, not from a statute.

The transfer fee is the one every seller should price first, because it is imposed by Wis. Stat. 77.22 on the grantor of real estate and is collected by the register of deeds when the deed goes in for recording. Recording itself costs a flat $30 under Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag). Everything else is negotiated, so ask the closing agent for a written estimate before you sign.

How much is the Wisconsin transfer fee on a home sale?

The fee is 30 cents for each $100 of value, with any fraction of $100 counted as a full $100. A $325,000 house produces 3,250 units of $100 and a fee of $975, and a $150,000 house produces $450.

Value has a precise meaning. Wis. Stat. 77.21(3) defines it, for any conveyance that is not a gift, as the full actual consideration paid or to be paid, including the amount of any lien on the property. For a gift, a deed for nominal consideration or an exchange, it is the estimated price the property would bring on the open market between a willing seller and a willing buyer. For a land contract, the value is the total principal the buyer agrees to pay the seller.

What are the main seller charges and deadlines in a Wisconsin closing?

The table below collects the amounts and time limits that Wisconsin law states directly.

ItemAmount or deadlineAuthority
Real estate transfer fee30 cents per $100 of value or fraction, charged to the grantorWis. Stat. 77.22(1)
Recording a deed$30 per documentWis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag)
Copy of a recorded document$2 first page, $1 each added page, $1 more to certifyWis. Stat. 59.43(2)(b)
Real estate condition report to buyerWithin 10 days after contract acceptanceWis. Stat. 709.02(1)
Mortgage payoff statement from lenderWithin 7 business days after a written request on residential propertyWis. Stat. 708.15(3)

Source: Wisconsin Legislature statute pages for each section listed.

Recording fees are payable in advance by the person who asks the register for the service.

Who is exempt from the Wisconsin transfer fee?

A conveyance is exempt only if it fits a category in Wis. Stat. 77.25, and the exemption must be named on the face of the deed. The categories most likely to apply to someone selling or transferring a house are:

  • A transfer by will, descent or survivorship.
  • A deed under a foreclosure, or in lieu of foreclosure, to a mortgage holder or a land contract seller.
  • A sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • A deed from a trustee to a beneficiary without actual consideration.
  • A deed that corrects or confirms a conveyance already recorded, given for nominal, inadequate or no consideration.
  • A deed that only gives or releases security for a debt that did not arise from a conveyance.
  • A conveyance under condemnation, or of real estate worth $1,000 or less.

A deed from a land contract seller is also exempt when the proper fee was paid at the time the land contract was recorded. Statute 77.256 bars a city, village, town or county from charging its own fee on an exempt conveyance.

What is the transfer return and who files it?

The transfer return is the Department of Revenue form that reports the value, the fee and any exemption, and it must be signed by both the grantor and the grantee. The register of deeds cannot accept the conveyance for recording until a completed return and the fee are in hand, unless the transfer falls under the narrow no-return rule in Wis. Stat. 77.255.

The state moved this form into My Tax Account in January 2026. The Department of Revenue's notice of January 12, 2026 says filers do not need a username or password and can file, view or amend a return. Title companies and attorneys generally file it for a sale. If you sign a deed on your own, use the department's RETR page for the guides and the exemption list.

Of the fee collected, 20 percent stays with the county and the rest goes to the state, according to Wis. Stat. 77.24. The department may later examine a return and assess more fee, or refund an overpayment, if the value was misreported or an exemption was claimed wrongly.

What does the seller's real estate condition report involve?

An owner who sells a property with one to four dwelling units must give the buyer a completed condition report within 10 days after the buyer's offer is accepted. The report is a statutory form in Wis. Stat. 709.03 that covers structural and mechanical systems, environmental matters, wells, septic systems and storage tanks, taxes and special assessments, permits, and land use.

If the buyer does not receive the report in time, the buyer may rescind the contract within two business days after the 10 days end and gets back any deposit. An owner who learns of information before acceptance that changes an answer must send an amended report or an amendment within 10 days of acceptance. The form states that it is not a warranty and does not replace inspections.

Some sellers are excused. Court-appointed fiduciaries, such as a personal representative, who never occupied the property do not complete it, and neither does an owner of property that has never been inhabited or a transfer that is exempt from the transfer fee. Chapter 709 reaches sales, exchanges and land contracts.

How does a mortgage payoff work at a Wisconsin closing?

You ask your lender in writing for a payoff statement, and on a loan secured by residential property the lender must send it within 7 business days. Wis. Stat. 708.15 says the statement must show the payoff amount on its date and the information needed to compute it on the requested payoff date, such as the per diem interest. It must also give the payment cutoff time and where and how to pay.

The request can name a payoff date up to 30 days out and may be made by an agent you authorize, such as the closing agent. On residential property a lender may not qualify the amount or say it can change before that date, which gives the closing agent a firm number. Request it early enough to fit your scheduled closing.

What should a Wisconsin seller ask the closing agent?

Ask for an itemized estimate before closing, and check each charge against the amounts above. A short list of questions covers most surprises:

  • What value is being reported on the transfer return, and does it include any lien being paid off?
  • Is any exemption being claimed, and under which subsection of Wis. Stat. 77.25?
  • What is the per diem on my mortgage, and what payoff date is the statement good through?
  • What is the balance on the property tax bill, and how is the current year prorated?
  • Which charges come from the contract, such as commission, title and any repair credits, and which come from statute?
  • Has the condition report been delivered, and on what date?

For the tax balance itself, ask the county treasurer or the municipal treasurer that bills the parcel. The property tax bill names the office that collects.

More questions about Wisconsin Closing Costs for Sellers

Who pays the real estate transfer fee in Wisconsin?

The seller does. Wis. Stat. 77.22 imposes the fee on the grantor at 30 cents per $100 of value, and the register of deeds collects it when the deed is submitted for recording.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Wisconsin?

The statutory recording fee is $30 per document under Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag). Copies of recorded documents are $2 for the first page and $1 for each added page, with $1 more to certify.

Is the transfer fee based on the sale price or the equity?

It is based on the sale price, not the equity. For a sale, value is the full consideration paid or to be paid, including the amount of any lien, so a house with a $200,000 mortgage and a $325,000 price is measured at $325,000.

When must I give the buyer the condition report?

Within 10 days after the buyer's offer is accepted. If the buyer does not get it in that window, the buyer has two more business days to rescind and recover any deposit.

How long does my lender have to send a payoff statement?

Seven business days after it receives your written request, on a loan secured by residential property. The statement must show the payoff amount and the per diem interest.

Where do I record a deed in Wisconsin?

Record it with the register of deeds in the county where the land sits. Under sec. 706.05, every conveyance and every other instrument affecting title to land in the state is entitled to record in the register of deeds office of each county where the affected land lies. If a deed covers parcels in two counties, it goes to both offices.

For transfer fee purposes the statute defines the register as the register of deeds for the county in which the particular real estate is located. The office keeps the recorded documents and their indexes permanently, and it makes certified or plain copies for a fee. Each county runs its own office, so look up its address, hours and rules for mail and electronic filing on the county website.

Recording is what puts a deed on the public record. Under sec. 706.08, a conveyance that is not recorded is void against a later purchaser in good faith and for valuable consideration whose conveyance is recorded first. A properly indexed document is treated as recorded as of the date and hour the general index shows it was accepted.

What does it cost to record a deed in Wisconsin?

The base recording fee is $30 per document, and a deed that transfers ownership usually carries a transfer fee as well. Both are due when you submit the deed, since the register of deeds collects fees in advance.

ItemAmountAuthority
Recording any document entitled to record$30Sec. 59.43(2)(ag)
Copy of a recorded document$2 for the first page, $1 for each added pageSec. 59.43(2)(b)
Certifying a copy$1 extraSec. 59.43(2)(b)
Subdivision, condominium or cemetery plat$50Sec. 59.43(2)(h)
Real estate transfer fee, paid by the grantor30 cents per $100 of value, or $3 per $1,000Sec. 77.22(1)

Source: Wis. Stat. 59.43 and Wis. Stat. 77.22, Wisconsin Legislature.

On a $250,000 sale, the transfer fee works out to $750 at 30 cents per $100. The transfer fee is measured on value, which for a sale means the full consideration paid including liens. The county keeps 20% of transfer fees and sends the rest to the state, and the register passes the fees and returns to the county treasurer by the 15th of each month. Some transfers owe no fee, and the register writes either the fee paid or the exemption reason, by subsection of sec. 77.25, on the deed.

What must a deed look like for a Wisconsin register of deeds to accept it?

It needs the right signatures, a valid form of authentication, a clear description of the land and parties, and a page layout that meets the format rules. The register of deeds may refuse a document that does not substantially comply with the standard format in sec. 59.43(2m).

  • The document name is clear and sits between 0.5 inch and 6 inches from the top of the first page.
  • The top right corner of page one has a blank 3 inch by 3 inch space inside the margins for the recording stamp. A document without it may not be recorded.
  • Page one carries return information, unless the document is recorded electronically.
  • Where the county requires a parcel identification number, each affected parcel is listed.
  • Paper is white, at least 20 pound, 8.5 inches wide and either 11 or 14 inches long.
  • The top margin of each page is 0.5 inch, and ink is black, blue or red.
  • Grantor, grantee, notaries and authenticators are clearly written or typed.

Beyond layout, sec. 706.05 asks for the signatures the law requires, an authentication form allowed by sec. 706.06 or ch. 140, and the land and parties identified so the entry can be indexed. A document that is to be indexed in the real estate records must carry the full legal description. The register may not deny recording for the absence of venue, seals, witnesses or other matter of form unless the law says otherwise. The register may not record a document that contains an individual's Social Security number.

What is the transfer return and who files it?

The real estate transfer return is the Department of Revenue form that reports the price, parties and parcel, and it must be completed before the register can accept most deeds. Under sec. 77.22(1), a completed return signed by both grantor and grantee and collection of the fee are prerequisites to acceptance of the conveyance for recording.

Returns are filed in the Department of Revenue's My Tax Account system, and no username or password is needed. The preparer picks the county, the document type from a list that includes warranty deed, quit claim deed, personal representative's deed, trustee's deed and land contract, and the conveyance date, which is the date the deed is signed and delivered. Both grantor and grantee must be listed, and spouses are entered as separate people. The preparer also enters the parcel number, property type, use, lot size and street address for each parcel.

The system prints a receipt number. To finish, take the printed receipt, the notarized deed and payment to the county register of deeds. Some counties accept this package electronically. The receipt number, the value and the last name of the grantor or grantee also let you view or amend the return later. For questions, the department lists RETR@wisconsin.gov and (608) 264-6885.

Accuracy matters. If the value is understated by 25% or more, or an exemption is claimed that does not apply, the department assesses the greater of $25 or 25% of the additional fee due.

What does the register of deeds do after I submit a deed?

The register records the document in the order received, marks it with the date, hour and minute, gives it a consecutive number and indexes it. Under sec. 59.43(1c), the register also shows on each conveyance the transfer fee paid or the reason for the exemption.

The register delivers the recorded document to the person you name as the authorized recipient when you provide adequate postage, unless you have a different agreement with the office. If you submit several documents as one transaction and any one fails the format rules, the register may return the whole group unrecorded. Check every document in the set before it goes in.

The office does not decide whether a price or an exemption is right. Under sec. 77.22(1), the register has no duty to determine the correct value or the validity of an exemption, so the sale price on the return should match the contract. The register can also give you certified or noncertified copies of anything recorded.

Does recording a deed matter when I sell my Wisconsin house?

Yes. The sale is not complete on the public record until the buyer's deed is recorded, and the order of recording decides priority between competing buyers. The closing agent normally handles this, but you should confirm who is submitting the deed and the transfer return.

Check that the legal description on the deed matches the one in your records and that the parcel number from your tax bill is on the document. Confirm that every owner on the title signs, that the notary block is complete and that nothing on the deed shows an individual's Social Security number. Ask the title company who pays the transfer fee, since the statute places it on the grantor, and ask for a copy of the recorded deed.

A cash sale of a Wisconsin house as-is follows the same recording steps as any other sale. Choose the buyer whose closing agent will explain the transfer return, the fees and the timeline in writing, and keep the transfer return receipt with your closing papers.

More questions about Wisconsin Recording a Deed

Who records a deed in Wisconsin?

The register of deeds of the county where the property is located records it. The buyer, a title company or the closing agent usually submits it, so confirm at closing who will.

How much is the Wisconsin recording fee?

The register of deeds charges $30 to record a document entitled to record. The grantor also owes a transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value unless the transfer is exempt. Plats cost $50.

Do I have to file a real estate transfer return before recording a deed?

In most cases yes. Sec. 77.22 makes a completed transfer return and collection of the fee prerequisites to recording, and the filing system flags document types that need no return. The Department of Revenue accepts the return in My Tax Account, and the register may accept the package electronically in some counties.

How long does recording take in Wisconsin?

Recording follows the order in which documents are received, and the register endorses the date, hour and minute. Ask your county register of deeds about current timing and any mail or electronic options.

What happens if I do not record my Wisconsin deed?

Under sec. 706.08, an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good faith purchaser for value whose conveyance is recorded first. Record the deed promptly so your ownership shows in the county records.
